checks.topic: Volumes of solids of revolution treated conceptually. Covers what the solid generated by revolving a plane region actually is, why each integrand is the area of a cross-section perpendicular to the axis, and where the radius is measured from. Covers why the washer integrand subtracts squared radii rather than squaring a difference, why the shell integrand carries a factor 2π and only one power of the radius, and how the position of the axis (x-axis, y-axis, y = k, x = h) changes each radius. Also covers when the variable of integration must be y, when the plain disk formula is legitimate, and the sign problem when the axis passes through the region.

questions.q: In the disk formula V = π∫ₐᵇ [f(x)]² dx, the factor π[f(x)]² is:
options: the circumference of the solid at x
the volume of the slice at x
the area of the circular cross-section cut by the plane through x perpendicular to the x-axis
the curved surface area of the solid between a and x
questions.concept: V = ∫A(s) ds: the integrand is a cross-sectional area, and dx supplies the thickness
questions.why: The plane through x perpendicular to the axis cuts a disk of radius f(x); its area is π[f(x)]², and multiplying by the thickness dx gives the volume element.

questions.q: A region with f(x) > g(x) > 0 on [a,b] is rotated about the x-axis. The volume is π∫ₐᵇ(f² − g²)dx and not π∫ₐᵇ(f − g)²dx because:
options: the cross-section is an annulus, and its area is the big disk's area minus the small disk's area — a difference of squares, whereas (f − g)² is the square of a difference
(f − g)² is harder to integrate, so the expanded form is preferred
the two expressions are equal, but the first is conventional
(f − g)² would give the area of the plane region rather than the volume
questions.concept: Washer cross-section: area of an annulus is πR² − πr², never π(R − r)²
questions.why: Removing the inner disk removes its area πr², so the annulus has area π(R² − r²); π(R − r)² is the area of a disk whose radius is the gap width, a different and always smaller quantity.

questions.q: A region lying entirely above the x-axis, under y = f(x) and above y = 0, is rotated about the line y = −2. The outer radius at x is:
options: f(x)
questions.concept: Radius is the distance from the axis of revolution to the boundary, not the coordinate value
questions.why: The far boundary sits at height f(x) and the axis at height −2, so the distance between them is f(x) − (−2) = f(x) + 2.

questions.q: The region between y = x and y = x² on [0,1] is rotated about the line y = 2. Which curve supplies the outer radius?
options: y = x, because it is the upper curve
y = x², because it is the curve farther from the line y = 2
neither — the radii are equal, so the volume is zero
y = x on [0, ½] and y = x² on [½, 1], since they swap over
questions.concept: Outer radius belongs to the boundary farthest from the axis, which need not be the upper curve
questions.why: With the axis above the region, the lower curve is the more distant one: 2 − x² > 2 − x on (0,1), so y = x² gives R and y = x gives r.

questions.q: In the shell formula dV = 2π·(radius)·(height)·dx, the factor 2π appears because:
options: unrolling the thin cylindrical shell gives a flat rectangle whose length is the shell's circumference, 2π × radius
each vertical strip generates two shells, one on each side of the axis
the area of a circle, πr², is doubled to account for both faces of the shell
the shell is swept through a full turn, and 2π converts degrees to radians
questions.concept: Shell element: a strip parallel to the axis sweeps a cylinder whose lateral area is 2π·radius·height
questions.why: Cut the thin cylinder down its side and flatten it: you get a rectangle of length 2π·radius and height h, with thickness dx, so dV = 2π·radius·height·dx.

questions.q: Using disks about the y-axis, a curve given as y = f(x) must first be rewritten as x = g(y) because:
options: integrals in y are always easier than integrals in x
the disk formula only accepts functions of y by convention
rotating about a vertical axis reverses the roles of the coordinates, so f must be replaced by its negative
the slices perpendicular to the y-axis are horizontal, so the disk radius must be expressed as a length measured in the x-direction at a given height y
questions.concept: The axis fixes the slicing direction, which fixes the variable of integration
questions.why: Disks must be cut perpendicular to the axis; for a vertical axis those cuts are horizontal, so both the radius and the thickness must be described in terms of y.

questions.q: The plain disk formula (rather than a washer) is legitimate exactly when:
options: the axis of revolution is horizontal
the region touches the axis of revolution along the whole interval, so the slices are full circles with no hole
the bounding function is non-negative on [a,b]
the region is bounded and the integrand is continuous
questions.concept: Disk vs washer is decided by whether the region reaches the axis (no hole) or is offset from it (hole)
questions.why: If the near boundary of the region sits away from the axis, revolution leaves a cylindrical cavity, and the disk formula would wrongly fill it in; only a region flush against the axis gives solid disks.

questions.q: The region under y = 4 − x², above the x-axis, from x = −2 to x = 2, is rotated about the y-axis. A student writes 2π∫₋₂² x(4 − x²)dx and obtains 0. The reason is:
options: the solid really has zero volume, since the region is symmetric about the y-axis
the height should have been squared, and squaring removes the sign problem
the shell radius is the distance |x|, so the negative half contributes a negative integrand; the left and right halves sweep the same solid, so one should integrate from 0 to 2 with radius x
the limits should be the y-values 0 and 4, not the x-values −2 and 2
questions.concept: Shell radius is a non-negative distance; a region straddling the axis sweeps each half onto the same solid
questions.why: For x < 0 the factor x is negative and cancels the right half; the correct radius is |x|, and since both halves generate the identical solid the volume is 2π∫₀²x(4 − x²)dx = 8π, not 0.

questions.q: Explain, in terms of what a cross-section of the solid actually looks like, why the washer integrand is π(R² − r²) and not π(R − r)². State what R and r mean.
questions.concept: Annulus area as a difference of disk areas; R and r as distances from the axis
questions.why: R is the distance from the axis of revolution to the boundary of the region farthest from it, r the distance to the nearest boundary. Slicing perpendicular to the axis gives an annulus — a disk of radius R with a concentric disk of radius r punched out — so its area is πR² − πr². π(R − r)² is instead the area of a single disk whose radius equals the width of the ring, a different figure; since R² − r² = (R − r)(R + r), the two agree only if R + r = R − r, i.e. r = 0.

questions.q: The disk integrand contains a squared radius but the shell integrand contains the radius only to the first power. Explain why, by saying what each element of volume is geometrically.
questions.concept: Disk element = area πR² times thickness; shell element = lateral surface 2πrh times thickness
questions.why: The disk element is a flat cylinder of radius R and thickness ds, so its volume is (πR²)·ds — the radius appears twice because a circular face is two-dimensional in the radius. The shell element is a thin hollow tube of radius r, height h and wall thickness ds, so its volume is (lateral area)·ds = (2πrh)·ds — here the radius contributes only through the circumference, one power. A dimension check confirms it: πR²·ds and 2πrh·ds are both length³, while squaring the shell radius would give length⁴.

questions.q: Explain how the axis of revolution fixes the variable of integration for the disk/washer method, and why the very same axis forces the opposite variable when you use shells.
questions.concept: Slices perpendicular to the axis (disks/washers) versus strips parallel to the axis (shells)
questions.why: Disks and washers are cut perpendicular to the axis, so consecutive slices are stacked along the axis: for a horizontal axis the slices advance in x (integrate dx), for a vertical axis they advance in y (integrate dy, with radii written as functions of y). Shells are built from strips parallel to the axis, so consecutive shells advance perpendicular to it: for a vertical axis the strips are vertical and advance in x (integrate dx), for a horizontal axis they are horizontal and advance in y. The axis therefore forces opposite variables for the two methods, which is why an awkward inversion in one method is often avoided by switching to the other.

questions.q: A region lies above y = 0 and below y = f(x) on [a,b]. Explain precisely what changes in the washer setup when the axis moves from the x-axis to the line y = k with k < 0, and explain why you cannot get the new volume by computing the volume about the x-axis and then adding a correction for the shift.
questions.concept: Shifting the axis changes both radii before squaring; the difference of squares is not translation-invariant
questions.why: About the x-axis the region is flush with the axis, so it is a disk problem with R = f(x), r = 0. About y = k with k < 0 the region no longer touches the axis, so a cylindrical hole appears: R = f(x) − k and r = 0 − k = −k, giving V = π∫ₐᵇ[(f − k)² − k²]dx = π∫ₐᵇ[f² − 2kf]dx. The extra term −2k∫f is not a constant offset — it depends on the function, i.e. on the area under f — so no fixed correction can be added to π∫f² dx. Both radii must be recomputed as distances from the new axis before squaring.

checks.topic: Faraday's law and Lenz's law as concepts. Covers what the flux rule actually asserts — that only a changing magnetic flux Φ_B = BA cos θ induces an emf, never the flux itself — and the meaning of θ as the angle from the loop's normal. Covers the physical content of the minus sign: the induced current opposes the CHANGE in flux, not the external field, together with the deck's three working rules and the right-hand grip rule for getting the sense of the current. Ends on the energy argument, that Lenz's law is conservation of energy rather than a separate empirical law.

questions.q: A bar magnet is held at rest with its north pole deep inside a wire loop connected to a sensitive ammeter. The ammeter reads exactly zero. The best explanation is:
options: The flux through the loop is large but constant, and only its rate of change drives an emf.
The flux through the loop is zero, because the magnet's field lines all return outside the loop.
There is an induced emf, but the loop's resistance is too large for the current to register.
The north and south poles of the magnet contribute equal and opposite flux, which cancels.
questions.concept: Faraday's law responds to dΦ/dt, not to Φ — a large steady flux gives no emf at all.
questions.why: The deck's Fig. c: with the magnet stationary the flux is large but unchanging, so dΦ_B/dt = 0 and ε = 0.

questions.q: In Φ_B = B*A*cos θ, the angle θ is measured between:
options: B and the plane of the loop.
B and the direction of the induced current.
B and the normal to the plane of the loop.
the normal to the loop and the induced magnetic field.
questions.concept: Definition of magnetic flux and the orientation angle; flux is maximum when the loop's plane is perpendicular to B.
questions.why: Flux is B·A with A the area vector along the outward normal, so θ is the angle between B and that normal.

questions.q: Which statement is the correct reading of the minus sign in ε = −N dΦ_B/dt?
options: The induced magnetic field inside the loop always points opposite to the external magnetic field.
The induced emf acts so as to oppose the change in flux that produced it.
The induced emf is always a negative quantity.
The induced current always flows opposite in sense to the current producing the external field.
questions.concept: Lenz's law is a statement about opposing the CHANGE, not about opposing the field.
questions.why: The induced effect opposes the change in flux; when the external flux is falling, the induced field actually points along the external field.

questions.q: A loop encloses a uniform field directed out of the page whose magnitude is steadily decreasing. The induced current is:
options: clockwise, since the induced field must be into the page — the induced field always opposes the external field.
zero, since a decreasing field cannot drive a current; only an increasing one can.
clockwise, from the right-hand grip rule applied with the thumb along the original external field.
counterclockwise, since the induced field is out of the page, replacing the flux that is being lost.
questions.concept: Applying the deck's rule 2 (falling flux → induced field along the original field) plus the right-hand grip rule.
questions.why: Falling out-of-page flux means the induced field inside the loop is out of the page, which by the grip rule is a counterclockwise current.

questions.q: Suppose that in some hypothetical world the induced current instead produced a field that *reinforced* an increasing external flux. The immediate consequence would be:
options: The induced emf would simply be twice as large, and energy would still be conserved.
The loop would be pushed towards the magnet, violating Newton's third law.
The flux change would reinforce itself, and the loop would deliver electrical energy indefinitely with nothing doing work on it.
Nothing inconsistent: Faraday's law would still hold, showing that Lenz's law is a logically independent rule.
questions.concept: The energy-conservation argument for the sign in Faraday's law.
questions.why: A reinforcing induced field is a runaway: the change feeds itself and energy appears from nowhere, which is why the sign must be negative.

questions.q: A magnet is pushed at a given speed towards a closed conducting loop, and then at the same speed towards an identical loop that has a small break cut in it. Comparing the force the hand must exert:
options: larger for the closed loop, because a current flows and the resulting magnetic force opposes the approach.
the same in both cases, because the induced emf is the same in both.
larger for the broken loop, because charge piles up at the break and repels the magnet.
zero in both cases, because magnetic forces do no work.
questions.concept: emf exists in both loops, but only a complete circuit carries current and therefore only it produces an opposing force; the work done is the source of the dissipated energy.
questions.why: The emf is the same, but current — and hence the Lenz opposing force and the work needed to push against it — requires the closed loop.

questions.q: A loop is positioned so that no field lines pass through the area it encloses, although the region just outside the loop contains a strong and rapidly changing field. The induced emf in the loop is:
options: large, because the field near the wire is strong and changing rapidly.
large, but confined to the sections of wire nearest the field region.
non-zero and constant in time, because the field outside contributes a fixed offset.
zero, because the emf depends only on the flux through the enclosed area.
questions.concept: The deck's rule that only the magnetic field within the loop counts; field outside the enclosed area is irrelevant.
questions.why: Faraday's law involves Φ_B through the enclosed area only, so a field entirely outside that area induces nothing.

questions.q: A circular loop is oriented so that a uniform magnetic field lies entirely *in the plane* of the loop. The magnitude of that field is then increased very rapidly. The induced emf is:
options: maximum, since dB/dt is large and the field lines lie as close to the wire as they can.
zero, since the flux through the loop is zero at every instant and so cannot change.
equal to A·dB/dt, since it is the magnitude of the field that changes, not the orientation.
zero, because the induced current would have nowhere to flow in this orientation.
questions.concept: A changing B does not by itself mean a changing flux — orientation can make the flux identically zero.
questions.why: With B in the plane of the loop, θ = 90° and Φ_B = BA cos90° = 0 at all times, so dΦ_B/dt = 0 however fast B changes.

questions.q: A loop is dragged at constant velocity across a region of *uniform* magnetic field: it enters, is briefly wholly inside, then leaves. Explain why a current flows while it enters and while it leaves, but not while it is wholly inside — even though the loop is moving the whole time and the field is present throughout.
questions.concept: Flux, not motion or field strength, is what must change; inside a uniform field a moving loop links constant flux.
questions.why: While entering, the area of the loop inside the field grows, so Φ_B increases and an emf is induced; while leaving, it shrinks and the emf reverses. Wholly inside, every part of the loop links the same uniform B and the enclosed flux is constant, so dΦ_B/dt = 0 and no current flows despite the motion. Motion matters only insofar as it changes the flux.

questions.q: In a rotating generator coil the emf is zero at the very instant the flux through the coil is maximum. Explain why, and say what the coil's orientation is at that instant.
questions.concept: emf tracks the slope of Φ(t), not its value: ε = NBAω sin(ωt) while Φ = BA cos(ωt).
questions.why: Φ = BA cos(ωt) is maximum when the coil's normal is parallel to B, i.e. the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field. At the peak of a cosine the slope is zero, so dΦ/dt = 0 and ε = 0. The emf is instead greatest a quarter-turn later, when the flux passes through zero and is changing fastest.

questions.q: Lenz's law is stated as "the induced effect opposes the *change* that caused it," not "opposes the external field." Using the case of a field out of the page that is decreasing, explain why those two statements are not the same, and which one is right.
questions.concept: Rule 2 of the deck: a falling flux induces a field in the SAME direction as the external field.
questions.why: With the external field out of the page and weakening, the induced current's field inside the loop is also out of the page — it reinforces the external field while opposing its decrease. The "opposes the field" version would wrongly predict a field into the page. Only the "opposes the change" version is correct; the two agree only when the flux is increasing.

questions.q: Explain, in terms of work and energy, why Lenz's law follows from conservation of energy rather than standing as an independent experimental rule of its own.
questions.concept: The minus sign as an energy statement: work must be done against the induced effect to sustain the flux change.
questions.why: Whatever causes the flux change — moving a magnet, sliding a rod — must work against the force exerted on the induced current, and that mechanical work is exactly what appears as I²R heating. If the induced current instead aided the change, the change would accelerate itself and both kinetic energy and heat would be produced with no source, which is impossible. Hence the sign is fixed by energy conservation, not by separate experiment.

checks.topic: The concepts of both Week 11 decks. Decomposition versus modularisation, module independence measured by cohesion and coupling, the single responsibility principle, information hiding and its benefits, refactoring, and horizontal versus vertical structural partitioning. From the second deck: the definition and purpose of software architecture, the three levels of software pattern (architectural, design, idiom), and the two generic design approaches. Questions target the precise wording of the definitions and the mechanism behind each claim rather than recognition of the vocabulary.

questions.q: The deck's definition of modularisation says each independent module "has everything it needs to implement only a part of the program's functionality." Which design does that clause rule out?
options: A module whose functions all serve a single aim but which is only 20 lines long
A module that is stored in its own file separate from the rest of the program
A module that is reused unchanged by a second, unrelated program
A module that implements one part of the functionality but must call into a sibling module's internals to obtain the data structures it works on
questions.concept: Definition of modularisation; independence clause
questions.why: "Has everything it needs" is the independence requirement: reaching into a sibling's internals means the module does not own what it needs, so it is not independent.

questions.q: Which of the following does the Decomposition and Modularisation deck list as a **disadvantage** of modularisation?
options: The negative impacts of a fault spread slowly through the system
The effects of a change in one component on other components are restricted
Compilation and loading time may be longer
Understanding a small module or function is easier
questions.concept: Disadvantages of modularisation
questions.why: Longer compilation and loading time is one of the five listed disadvantages; a and b are benefits of structural partitioning and information hiding, and d is an advantage.

questions.q: A developer changes the internal date format inside module `Billing`. Three other modules stop compiling and must be edited. Which property of the design does this observation most directly measure, and in which direction?
options: Coupling between `Billing` and those modules, and it is high
Cohesion of `Billing`, and it is low
Cohesion of `Billing`, and it is high, since one change touched one aim
Coupling between `Billing` and those modules, and it is low, since only three modules were affected
questions.concept: Coupling as a between-module measure
questions.why: Coupling is the extent to which modules depend on other modules before performing their function; a change rippling outward is a dependence on Billing's internals, so coupling is high.

questions.q: According to the deck, information hiding requires that modules pass to each other
options: all of their data structures, but only through a documented public interface
only that much information which is required to accomplish the software functions
the processing details of any function whose result the other module consumes
nothing at all, since a truly independent module never communicates
questions.concept: Information hiding
questions.why: The deck's wording is exactly "they pass only that much information to each other, which is required to accomplish the software functions"; a documented interface that still exposes all data structures is not information hiding.

questions.q: A design model yields a component that performs four functions having a limited relationship with one another. What is the deck's prescribed response, and its stated payoff?
options: Leave the component whole, since keeping the four functions in one place minimises the coupling in the system
Hide the four functions behind a single controlled interface, so that information hiding compensates for the weak relationship between them
Refactor the component into four different components, each exhibiting high cohesion, which leads to easier integration, testing and maintenance
Merge the component into each of its callers, so that the weakly related functions become internal details of those callers
questions.concept: Refactoring worked example; low cohesion
questions.why: This is the deck's own example: split the low-cohesion component into four high-cohesion components, giving easier integration, testing and maintenance; hiding or merging leaves the cohesion defect intact.

questions.q: What does the deck give as the specific cost of **horizontal** partitioning?
options: Decision-making sinks into the worker modules, so faults are hard to localise
Control modules end up performing input, computation and output as well as deciding
The hierarchy becomes so deep that compilation and loading time increase
More data must be passed across the module interface, making the control flow more complex, especially where data moves rapidly from one function to another
questions.concept: Horizontal structural partitioning
questions.why: The deck names exactly this cost; the other options describe failures of vertical partitioning or a disadvantage of modularisation generally.

questions.q: In vertical partitioning, which statement matches the deck's description of the division of labour?
options: Control modules at the top perform the decision-making and do little processing; worker modules at the low level perform all input, computation and output
Control modules at the top perform input and computation; worker modules at the low level decide which functions to execute
Every module both decides and processes, so that no single module becomes a bottleneck
Control modules communicate between functions and execute those functions on their behalf
questions.concept: Vertical structural partitioning
questions.why: Decision at the top with little processing, all input/computation/output at the bottom; option d is the deck's description of horizontal partitioning.

questions.q: Which mapping of the three pattern levels matches the deck?
options: Architectural = medium-level, often equivalent to software components; design = high-level; idiom = language-independent

Architectural = high-level, often considered equivalent to software architecture; design = medium-level, often considered equivalent to software components; idiom = low-level and programming-language specific
Architectural = high-level; design = low-level and language specific; idiom = medium-level coding conventions
All three are language-specific, differing only in how many components they govern
questions.concept: Architectural pattern, design pattern, idiom
questions.why: High/medium/low with architectural equated to software architecture, design equated to software components, and only the idiom being language-specific ("coding patterns").

questions.q: The deck says the meaning of decomposition is "actually embedded in the definition of modularisation." Explain the relationship precisely, and describe a case that is decomposition but not successful modularisation.
questions.concept: Decomposition versus modularisation
questions.why: Modularisation is dividing a program's functionality into independent modules, each holding everything it needs for its part; the act of separating the code into different modules and functions is itself decomposition, so decomposition is the breaking-apart contained inside modularisation. A case that is decomposition but not modularisation: chopping a 5,000-line function into ten files that all read and write the same shared globals and must be changed together. The application has been broken up, but the pieces are not independent, so cohesion is low and coupling is high and none of the promised benefits follow.

questions.q: Modularisation is meant to make change cheap, yet the deck lists "demands more initial design time" and "inter-module communication problems may be increased" as disadvantages. Explain the mechanism by which the same act of splitting produces both the benefit and these two costs.
questions.concept: Advantages versus disadvantages of modularisation
questions.why: Splitting works by creating boundaries: once functionality lives behind an interface, a change on one side stops at that boundary instead of propagating, which is the cheap-change benefit. But the boundaries have to be chosen before any code is written, and choosing them is the extra initial design effort, because a badly placed boundary must be cut through later. The same boundaries also convert what used to be free in-process access into explicit traffic across interfaces, so there are now more interfaces to define, agree, version and get wrong: that is the increase in inter-module communication problems, along with the longer execution and loading times the deck also lists.

questions.q: Explain why information hiding is the mechanism that makes low coupling achievable, rather than a separate nicety. Refer to the deck's three stated benefits of information hiding in your reasoning.
questions.concept: Information hiding and coupling
questions.why: Coupling is the extent to which a module depends on other modules before it can do its work; a module can only depend on what it can see. Information hiding makes the data structures and processing details of a module inaccessible to others and lets only the required information cross, so it removes the very things another module could come to depend on. That is why its three benefits are the coupling story restated: communication through controlled interfaces means dependence is confined to a narrow agreed surface; a decreased probability of adverse effects follows because nobody is relying on internals that may change; and the effects of a change in one component on others are restricted because a change behind the interface is invisible outside it.

questions.q: The deck states that top-down and bottom-up design "are not individually practicable" and that in bottom-up design "with each higher level, the amount of abstraction is increased." Explain why each approach alone fails, and why the abstraction remark explains which approach suits a system built from an existing system.
questions.concept: Top-down and bottom-up design approaches
questions.why: Pure top-down keeps decomposing a general model into more specific parts, but the decomposition is a guess about what the lowest level can actually provide; if the available primitives do not match, the whole hierarchy has to be redrawn. Pure bottom-up composes higher-level components from basic ones, but with no view of the whole system there is nothing to say which higher-level components are the right ones to build, so effort can be spent on parts that never fit together. Hence the deck's combination. The abstraction remark explains bottom-up's home ground: when a system is created from an existing system, the basic primitives already exist and each composition step raises the abstraction level over them, so the design grows upward from known material rather than downward into unknown detail, which is where top-down belongs.

checks.topic: The same volumes-of-revolution material worked as problems. Covers locating the limits of integration by solving for the intersections of the bounding curves, choosing between integrating in x and in y, and evaluating disk, washer and shell integrals to a number. Covers rotation about lines other than the coordinate axes (y = −1, y = 2, x = 4) where every radius must be rewritten as a distance from the axis. Also covers splitting a region when the bounding curve changes partway, cross-checking a shell answer against a washer answer, and the sign and ordering traps that produce negative or too-small volumes.

questions.q: The region under y = 2x, above y = 0, from x = 0 to x = 3, is rotated about the x-axis. The volume is
options: 9π
questions.concept: Disk method about the x-axis: square the function before integrating
questions.why: π∫₀³(2x)²dx = 4π[x³/3]₀³ = 36π; 9π is π∫₀³2x dx, the result of forgetting to square.

questions.q: The region between y = x and y = x² is rotated about the x-axis. The volume is
questions.concept: Washer with R = x, r = x² on [0,1]
questions.why: π∫₀¹(x² − x⁴)dx = π(1/3 − 1/5) = 2π/15; π/30 is the π∫(R − r)² trap and π/6 is the volume about the y-axis.

questions.q: The region under y = x², above y = 0, from x = 0 to x = 2, is rotated about the line y = −1. The volume is
questions.concept: Shifted axis: R = x² + 1 and r = 1, both measured from y = −1
questions.why: π∫₀²[(x² + 1)² − 1]dx = π(32/5 + 16/3) = 176π/15; 206π/15 forgets the inner radius r = 1 and 32π/5 is the volume about the x-axis.

questions.q: The region bounded by y = x², x = 0 and y = 4 (first quadrant) is rotated about the y-axis. The volume is
options: 8π
4π
questions.concept: Disks in y about a vertical axis, radius x = √y
questions.why: π∫₀⁴(√y)²dy = π∫₀⁴y dy = 8π; shells confirm it: 2π∫₀²x(4 − x²)dx = 8π.

questions.q: The region bounded by y = x² and y = 2x is rotated about the x-axis. The volume is
questions.concept: Limits from x² = 2x, then washer with R = 2x, r = x²
questions.why: The curves meet at x = 0 and x = 2, and π∫₀²(4x² − x⁴)dx = π(32/3 − 32/5) = 64π/15; 16π/15 is the π∫(R − r)² trap and 8π/3 is the volume about the y-axis.

questions.q: The region bounded by y = √x and y = x/2 is to be rotated about the x-axis. The limits of integration in x are
options: 0 and 2
0 and 4
0 and 1
−2 and 2
questions.concept: Limits come from solving the curves simultaneously, not from the sketch
questions.why: √x = x/2 gives x = x²/4, so x² − 4x = 0 and x = 0 or 4; 0 and 2 are the corresponding y-values, not x-values.

questions.q: The region under y = √x, above y = 0, from x = 0 to x = 4, is rotated about the line y = 2. The volume is
options: 8π
questions.concept: Axis above the region: R = 2 (from y = 0) and r = 2 − √x (from the curve)
questions.why: π∫₀⁴[4 − (2 − √x)²]dx = π∫₀⁴(4√x − x)dx = π(64/3 − 8) = 40π/3; 8π is what π∫(R − r)² gives.

questions.q: The region under y = x², above y = 0, from x = 0 to x = 2, is rotated about the line x = 4. Using shells, the volume is
options: 8π
questions.concept: Shell radius about a vertical line x = h is the distance |x − h|, here 4 − x
questions.why: 2π∫₀²(4 − x)x²dx = 2π(32/3 − 4) = 40π/3; 8π comes from using radius x (axis not shifted) and 88π/3 from using x + 4.

questions.q: The triangle bounded by y = x, y = 2 − x and y = 0 is rotated about the y-axis. Set up the shell integral(s) in x and explain why the setup must be split, then explain why the washer setup in y needs no split. Give the volume.
questions.concept: Splitting is forced by a change of bounding curve in the chosen variable; the other variable may avoid it
questions.why: The top boundary of the triangle is y = x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 and y = 2 − x for 1 ≤ x ≤ 2, so a vertical strip has height x on the first piece and 2 − x on the second: V = 2π∫₀¹x·x dx + 2π∫₁²x(2 − x)dx = 2π/3 + 4π/3 = 2π. Integrating in y, every horizontal strip runs from x = y on the left to x = 2 − y on the right for all y in [0,1], so one washer integral suffices: V = π∫₀¹[(2 − y)² − y²]dy = π∫₀¹(4 − 4y)dy = 2π. Same answer, no split.

questions.q: The region bounded by y = x² and y = 2x is rotated about the y-axis. Write both the shell integral in x and the washer integral in y, explain why they are obliged to agree, and give the common value.
questions.concept: Two slicings of one solid must give the same volume; use one as a check on the other
questions.why: Curves meet at (0,0) and (2,4). Shells in x: radius x, height 2x − x², so V = 2π∫₀²x(2x − x²)dx = 2π(16/3 − 4) = 8π/3. Washers in y: at height y the region runs from x = y/2 (the line) out to x = √y (the parabola), so R = √y, r = y/2 and V = π∫₀⁴(y − y²/4)dy = π(8 − 16/3) = 8π/3. They must agree because both are exact decompositions of the same solid — one into nested tubes, the other into stacked rings — and volume does not depend on how you slice it.

questions.q: A student computes the volume of the region between y = x and y = x² rotated about y = 2 as π∫₀¹[(2 − x)² − (2 − x²)²]dx and gets −8π/15. Explain exactly what went wrong and give the correct volume.
questions.concept: The outer radius is the distance to the farther boundary, which reverses when the axis lies above the region
questions.why: The student assumed the upper curve y = x gives the outer radius. With the axis at y = 2, above the whole region, the more distant boundary is the lower curve y = x²: 2 − x² > 2 − x on (0,1). So R = 2 − x², r = 2 − x, and the radii were interchanged, which negates the integrand. The correct volume is π∫₀¹[(2 − x²)² − (2 − x)²]dx = π∫₀¹(4x − 5x² + x⁴)dx = π(2 − 5/3 + 1/5) = 8π/15. A negative answer is always a sign the radii were swapped, since a volume cannot be negative.

questions.q: The region bounded by y = √x, y = 0 and x = 4 is rotated about the y-axis. Explain how you choose the variable of integration, set the problem up both ways (shells in x and washers in y), say why the inner radius in the y-setup is y² and not √y, and give the volume.
questions.concept: Choosing the variable; inverting the boundary correctly when integrating in y
questions.why: The axis is vertical, so shells use vertical strips and integrate in x, while washers must be cut horizontally and integrate in y. Shells: radius x, height √x, giving V = 2π∫₀⁴x^(3/2)dx = 2π(2/5)(32) = 128π/5. Washers: at height y (0 ≤ y ≤ 2) the strip runs from the curve on the left to the line x = 4 on the right, so R = 4 and r = y², and V = π∫₀²(16 − y⁴)dy = π(32 − 32/5) = 128π/5. The inner radius is y² because inverting y = √x gives x = y²; writing √y confuses the function with its inverse and would be dimensionally and numerically wrong (at y = 2 the curve is at x = 4, not x = √2).

checks.topic: The same Faraday/Lenz material worked numerically. Computing induced emf from a rate of change of B in an N-turn coil, evaluating Φ = BA cos θ when the question specifies the angle to the loop's PLANE, and motional emf ε = BLv with its induced current I = ε/R and retarding force F = B²L²v/R. Also generator output, ε_peak = NBAω with ω = 2πf and ε_rms = ε_peak/√2, and the time-independent circulated charge q = N|ΔΦ|/R. Emphasis throughout on the unit, angle, 2π and current-sense traps.

questions.q: A 50-turn coil of area 4.0×10⁻³ m² has its plane perpendicular to a uniform field that rises steadily from 0.20 T to 0.80 T in 0.30 s. The magnitude of the induced emf is:
questions.concept: ε = N·A·dB/dt — use the RATE of change of B, and do not drop the number of turns.

questions.q: A flat loop of area 0.020 m² sits in a uniform 0.50 T field with the *plane of the loop* inclined at 30° to the field. The flux through the loop is:
options: zero, because B is not perpendicular to the loop
questions.concept: θ in BA cos θ is measured from the normal, so a plane at 30° to B means θ = 60°.
questions.why: Φ = BA cos60° = 0.50 × 0.020 × 0.500 = 5.0×10⁻³ Wb; using cos30° gives the wrong 8.7×10⁻³ Wb.

questions.q: A rod of length 0.50 m slides on rails at 4.0 m/s perpendicular to a 0.30 T field, the field being perpendicular to the plane of the circuit. The circuit's total resistance is 2.0 Ω. The induced current is:
questions.concept: Motional emf ε = BLv followed by Ohm's law I = ε/R.
questions.why: ε = 0.30 × 0.50 × 4.0 = 0.60 V, so I = 0.60/2.0 = 0.30 A (0.60 is the emf in volts, not the current).

questions.q: The rod in question 3 is now pulled at 8.0 m/s instead of 4.0 m/s, everything else unchanged. The retarding magnetic force on the rod and the power dissipated in the resistance, respectively:
options: both double
the force doubles, the power quadruples
the force quadruples, the power doubles
both quadruple
questions.concept: Scaling of F = B²L²v/R (linear in v) against P = B²L²v²/R = Fv (quadratic in v).
questions.why: ε, I and hence F = BIL all scale as v, but the power P = Fv carries a second factor of v, so it goes as v².

questions.q: A 200-turn coil of area 0.015 m² rotates at 60 revolutions per second in a uniform 0.40 T field, about an axis perpendicular to the field. The peak emf is about:
questions.concept: ε_peak = NBAω with ω = 2πf in rad/s — the commonest slip is using f in place of ω.
questions.why: ω = 2π(60) = 377 rad/s, so ε_peak = 200 × 0.40 × 0.015 × 377 = 4.5×10² V ≈ 452 V (72 V comes from using f directly).

questions.q: For the generator of question 5, the rms emf is about:
questions.concept: ε_rms = ε_peak/√2 for a sinusoidal output — not half the peak, and not √2 times it.
questions.why: 452/√2 = 320 V; 226 V would be half the peak and 640 V would be √2 times it.

questions.q: The flux through each turn of a 100-turn coil of total resistance 20 Ω is changed by 0.040 Wb. The total charge that circulates round the coil is:
options: 0.20 C, but only if the change takes exactly 1.0 s; proportionally more if it is faster
2.0 C, whatever the duration of the change
0.20 C, whatever the duration of the change
indeterminate unless the time taken for the change is given
questions.concept: q = ∫I dt = N|ΔΦ|/R contains no time — a faster change gives a larger current for a shorter time.
questions.why: q = 100 × 0.040/20 = 0.20 C, independent of how long the flux change takes.

questions.q: A rod slides to the right along horizontal rails, so that the circuit's enclosed area is increasing; the uniform field is directed into the page. Which is correct?
options: The induced current is clockwise, and the magnetic force on the rod points left, opposing the motion.
The induced current is counterclockwise, and the magnetic force on the rod points right, aiding the motion.
The induced current is clockwise, and the force on the rod is zero, since it carries current parallel to B.
The induced current is counterclockwise, and the magnetic force on the rod points left, opposing the motion.
questions.concept: Fixing the sense of the induced current from Lenz's law, then checking that F = BIL comes out opposing the motion.
questions.why: Into-page flux is increasing, so the induced field inside the loop is out of the page — a counterclockwise current — and the resulting force on the rod necessarily retards it.

questions.q: The flux through a coil goes from 0 to 0.30 Wb in 0.20 s, but not at a uniform rate. State what N|ΔΦ|/Δt gives you here, what it cannot tell you, and describe one situation in which the instantaneous emf would be many times larger than that figure.
questions.concept: Average emf N|ΔΦ|/Δt versus instantaneous emf N dΦ/dt.
questions.why: N|ΔΦ|/Δt gives only the AVERAGE emf over the 0.20 s (1.5 V per turn here); it says nothing about the emf at any particular instant, nor about the peak. If almost all of the flux change is squeezed into a few milliseconds — a switch opened, or a magnet snatched away at the end of the interval — the instantaneous dΦ/dt over that short window, and hence ε, is many times the average.

questions.q: For the rod of question 3 (B = 0.30 T, L = 0.50 m, v = 4.0 m/s, R = 2.0 Ω), work out the retarding force and show numerically that the mechanical power supplied equals the electrical power dissipated. Explain why this equality would fail if the induced current ran the other way.
questions.concept: Energy bookkeeping in the sliding-rod circuit: P_mech = Fv = I²R.
questions.why: ε = BLv = 0.60 V, I = 0.30 A, F = BIL = 0.30 × 0.30 × 0.50 = 0.045 N. Mechanical power = Fv = 0.045 × 4.0 = 0.18 W; electrical power = I²R = (0.30)² × 2.0 = 0.18 W — equal. If the current ran the other way, the force would drive the rod forward instead of retarding it, so the rod would gain kinetic energy while ALSO dissipating 0.18 W of heat, with nothing supplying either.

questions.q: A student doubles the number of turns on a coil in a given changing field, using the same wire, so that the coil's resistance doubles too. Explain what happens to the induced emf, to the induced current, and to the charge circulated by a given flux change, and why those three answers are not all the same.
questions.concept: How N enters ε = N dΦ/dt, I = ε/R and q = NΔΦ/R when R itself scales with N.
questions.why: The emf doubles, since ε = N dΦ_B/dt is proportional to N. The current does NOT change: I = ε/R has both numerator and denominator doubled. The charge q = N|ΔΦ|/R likewise stays the same, for the same reason. The emf depends on N alone, while the current and charge depend on the ratio N/R, which the extra turns leave untouched.

questions.q: A generator's rotation frequency is doubled, with the same coil and the same field. State what happens to ε_peak, to ε_rms, and to the average emf over one complete cycle, and explain why one of those three answers is different in kind from the other two.
questions.concept: ε_peak = NBAω ∝ f and ε_rms = ε_peak/√2 ∝ f, but the mean of a full sine cycle is identically zero.
questions.why: ε_peak = NBAω = 2πfNBA doubles, and ε_rms = ε_peak/√2 doubles with it. The average over one complete cycle is zero both before and after, because ε = ε_peak sin(ωt) spends equal time positive and negative and the two halves cancel exactly. That is why rms, not the plain average, is the useful measure of an a.c. output.

checks.topic: The same Week 11 material applied to concrete design judgements rather than recalled. Students read short module listings and pseudocode and decide whether a module is cohesive, what it is coupled to and why, which principle a design violates, and how to redraw the boundaries. Scenarios cover judging cohesion from a function list, spotting coupling through a shared data structure, evaluating what a proposed refactor buys and costs, checking a hierarchy against vertical partitioning, choosing top-down or bottom-up for a given project, and deciding whether a change qualifies as refactoring at all.

questions.q:
Consider this module:

```
module AccountUtils:
    validate_email(address)
    compute_payroll_tax(employee, year)
    send_confirmation_email(user)
    resize_avatar_image(file, width, height)
```

The best diagnosis is:
options: High cohesion and high coupling, because all four functions concern users
Low coupling, therefore high cohesion, since the two always move together
Acceptable cohesion, because each individual function has a single responsibility
Low cohesion, because the functions do not work together towards one ultimate aim of the module, whatever their coupling to other modules
questions.concept: Judging cohesion from a module's function list
questions.why: Cohesion asks whether the functions in the module work together towards the module's ultimate aim; these four do not, and cohesion is judged independently of coupling. Option d confuses per-function responsibility with module cohesion.

questions.q:
```
module Inventory:
    stock_level = { }          # sku -> integer

module OrderProcessor:
    place_order(sku, n):
        Inventory.stock_level[sku] = Inventory.stock_level[sku] - n
        ...
```

Which judgement is correct?
options: Coupling is low, because `OrderProcessor` calls no function of `Inventory`
Coupling is high, because `OrderProcessor` depends on `Inventory`'s internal data structure before it can perform its function, which is exactly what information hiding forbids
Cohesion of `Inventory` is low, because it stores data instead of performing functions
This is good vertical partitioning: `OrderProcessor` decides and `Inventory` merely holds data
questions.concept: Coupling through a shared data structure; information hiding
questions.why: Calling no function is not independence: reaching into another module's data structure is the strongest form of dependence, and the deck forbids one module accessing another's data structures and processing details.

questions.q: A component performing four weakly related functions is split into four high-cohesion components. Using only what the decks state, what does this buy and what does it cost?
options: Buys easier integration, testing and maintenance; costs possible longer execution time, larger storage, longer compilation and loading, and more inter-module communication
Buys reduced execution time and smaller storage; costs a loss of information hiding
Buys lower coupling automatically; costs nothing, since external behaviour is unchanged
Buys easier testing; costs a violation of the single responsibility principle, since responsibility is now spread across four modules
questions.concept: Refactoring payoff weighed against the disadvantages of modularisation
questions.why: The payoff is the deck's refactoring example; the price is its list of modularisation disadvantages. Coupling is not automatically lowered by splitting, and four single-responsibility modules honour the principle rather than violating it.

questions.q:
```
module ReportRunner:                  # top of the hierarchy
    run():
        rows = read_csv("sales.csv")
        totals = sum_by_region(rows)
        print_table(totals)

module Constants:                     # bottom of the hierarchy
    REGIONS = [...]
```

Judged against the deck's description of vertical partitioning, the defect is:
options: None: the top module correctly communicates between functions and executes them
`Constants` should be at the top, since values are decided before they are used
The top-level control module is doing all the input, computation and output, which the deck assigns to low-level worker modules; the top should be deciding and processing little
The hierarchy is too shallow, so horizontal partitioning should be used instead
questions.concept: Applying vertical partitioning to a hierarchy
questions.why: Vertical partitioning puts decision-making with little processing at the top and all input, computation and output in worker modules; here the control module does the work itself. Option a describes horizontal partitioning, which is a different scheme, not a defence of this one.

questions.q: A team must build a new analytics service on top of an existing, well-tested set of data-access and statistics primitives already in use elsewhere in the company. Which approach does the deck say is more suitable, and why?
options: Bottom-up, because a system created from an existing system can compose higher-level components from basic primitives, with abstraction increasing at each higher level
Top-down, because the service is new and must first be seen as one whole entity
Top-down, because the specific details of the primitives are already known
Bottom-up, because bottom-up design avoids the extra initial design time that modularisation demands
questions.concept: Choosing between top-down and bottom-up for a given project
questions.why: The deck assigns bottom-up to systems created from an existing system whose basic primitives can be reused; option c inverts the deck's rule, which puts top-down where specific details are unknown.

questions.q: A pull request titled "refactor `charge_card`" both extracts the retry logic into a helper and changes the function so that on a network timeout it now returns `PENDING` where it previously returned `FAILED`. Under the deck's definition, this is
options: refactoring, because the internal structure was improved and the helper raised cohesion
refactoring, because the caller can be updated to handle the new value
not refactoring, because the external behaviour of the system has been changed
not refactoring, because refactoring may never introduce a new module or helper
questions.concept: The boundary of the definition of refactoring
questions.why: Refactoring improves internal structure without changing external behaviour; a changed return value is changed external behaviour, and improving structure at the same time does not rescue it.

questions.q:
Two candidate interfaces for the same feature:

```
A:  render_post_summary(db_connection, cursor, raw_row_dict, template_cache)
B:  render_post_summary(post_id) -> string
```

Which is preferred and on what stated grounds?
options: A, because passing the connection avoids a second lookup and so shortens execution time
A, because more parameters make the dependency explicit and therefore reduce coupling
B, but only if `render_post_summary` is the sole function in its module
B, because it passes only that much information as is required to accomplish the function and keeps the caller from touching internal data structures
questions.concept: Information hiding expressed in an interface
questions.why: Signature B passes only what the function needs; A forces the caller to hold connections, cursors and raw rows, which is dependence on internals. Making a dependency explicit documents coupling, it does not reduce it.

questions.q: A monolithic 5,000-line function is split into 30 modules stored in separate files. Which outcome is *not* predicted by the decks?
options: Different people can now work on different parts of the program
Storage size may increase and loading time may lengthen
Every module is now independent, because separate files cannot depend on each other
A change to one part is less likely to affect the other parts
questions.concept: What file separation does and does not guarantee
questions.why: Separate files are a packaging fact, not independence; independence comes from each module owning what it needs and hiding its internals. The other three are stated advantages and disadvantages.

questions.q:
You inherit this module:

```
module UserManager:
    register(user)
    login(email, password)
    send_marketing_newsletter()
    backup_database()
```

State whether it is cohesive, give the specific refactor you would perform, and explain what property of each resulting module the refactor is aimed at — not merely that it becomes "cleaner".
questions.concept: Diagnosing cohesion and prescribing the refactor
questions.why: It is not cohesive: register and login serve the module's aim of managing user identity, but sending marketing newsletters and backing up the database have only a limited relationship to that aim or to each other. Following the deck's refactoring example, split it into a user-management module holding register and login, a marketing or notification module, and an operations or backup module. The property aimed at is high cohesion in each resulting module, so that every function in a module works towards that module's single ultimate aim, and by the single responsibility principle no module carries more than one responsibility. The stated payoff is easier integration, testing and maintenance, since a change to the newsletter can no longer force retesting of login.

questions.q: In question 2, suppose you replace the direct write with a call `Inventory.reduce_stock(sku, n)`. Explain why this genuinely lowers coupling rather than simply relocating the dependency, and name what `OrderProcessor` is now permitted to know about `Inventory`.
questions.concept: Reducing coupling by imposing an interface
questions.why: The dependency does not disappear, but it changes kind: OrderProcessor previously depended on a data structure, so any change to how stock is represented — a dictionary becoming a database table, or per-warehouse counts — broke it. It now depends only on a named operation whose meaning is stable, so Inventory can change its internals freely, which is precisely the information hiding benefit of restricting the effects of change in one component on others. What OrderProcessor is permitted to know is the interface alone: the operation's name, the sku and quantity it takes, and what it returns or signals when stock is insufficient. It is not permitted to know the representation of stock_level or how the reduction is carried out.

questions.q: You are decomposing the user-registration feature of a social media platform into validating the user's input, creating a new user account, and sending a confirmation email. Explain the criterion you would use to group these and other subproblems into modules such as user management, post management and following management, and justify that criterion using cohesion and coupling rather than by appeal to tidiness.
questions.concept: Choosing module boundaries during decomposition
questions.why: The criterion is to group subproblems that operate on the same data and serve the same ultimate aim, so that user-account subproblems land in user management, post subproblems in post management and follow-graph subproblems in following management. This maximises cohesion, because every function inside a module then works towards that module's one aim, and it minimises coupling, because the data a group of subproblems shares stays inside one module instead of crossing interfaces. Grouping instead by technical similarity — putting every validation together, every email together — would scatter one feature across many modules, so a change to registration would touch several modules at once: low cohesion and high coupling in one move. Note that sending the confirmation email is a candidate for a shared notification module, since it serves every feature rather than user management alone.

questions.q: After splitting a working monolith into forty small modules, a team finds request latency has risen, the build takes three times as long, and two teams keep breaking each other's interfaces. Explain which of the deck's stated disadvantages of modularisation these are, and argue — using cohesion — whether the split was wrong in principle or wrong in where the boundaries were drawn.
questions.concept: Weighing the disadvantages of modularisation against boundary placement
questions.why: The three symptoms map onto three of the deck's five listed disadvantages: execution time may be longer, compilation and loading time may be longer, and inter-module communication problems may be increased. The split is not wrong in principle, since those costs are predicted for any modularisation and are paid for by understandability, parallel work and cheaper change. The diagnosis lies in cohesion: modules whose functions genuinely work together toward one aim keep their chatter internal, so a well-placed boundary carries little traffic and a stable interface. Constant interface breakage and heavy cross-module calls are evidence that closely related functions were separated, that is, that cohesion was cut through. The remedy is to merge the fragments that keep changing together back into one cohesive module rather than to abandon modularisation.

recapCandidates.topic: Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the CHANGE in flux, not the field itself, so a decreasing field is helped by the induced field rather than fought; the minus sign in emf = -N dPhi/dt is conservation of energy written down, and the direction is always read from the induced field required INSIDE the loop.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: "Opposes" is read as "opposes the field", which happens to give the right answer for every approaching-magnet demonstration and silently reverses the current in every receding, switching-off or collapsing-field case.
whyQuestions: Why, when a north pole is pushed towards a loop, does the loop's near face have to become a north pole - and which quantity is it that the induced current is set up to oppose?
Why does that same reasoning give an induced field pointing along the external field when the magnet is pulled away, even though the law is stated as "opposition"?
Why must the sign be negative - what could you build, and what would it produce, if the induced current reinforced the change instead?
Why does the direction have to be read from the field the induced current makes inside the loop, when the same current makes a field outside the loop too, pointing the other way?

Why does the retarding force on a rod sliding on rails always oppose the motion, whichever direction the rod moves and whichever way B points - and why is the energy audit F*v = I^2*R the same statement as the minus sign?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
States the law with its correct object - the induced field opposes THE CHANGE in the flux through the loop, so a rising external flux is met by an opposing induced field, a falling one by an aiding induced field, and a steady flux however large induces nothing.
Derives the minus sign from energy rather than asserting it: a reinforcing induced effect would amplify its own cause and deliver energy from nothing, which is also why the magnetic force retards whatever motion produces the emf.
Names and runs the procedure: identify the external flux through the enclosed area and whether it is growing or shrinking, deduce the induced field required INSIDE the loop, then apply the right-hand grip rule - the field outside the loop is irrelevant.
recapCandidates.workedExample: One loop flat in the page, four situations. (1) B out of the page rising 0.20 -> 0.60 T: induced field into the page, current CLOCKWISE - the case everybody gets right. (2) B out of the page falling 0.60 -> 0.20 T: the field direction is identical, only the sign of dPhi/dt differs, so the induced field is OUT of the page and the current is COUNTERCLOCKWISE; the wrong approach reasons "oppose the field, so into the page, so clockwise" and reproduces answer (1) exactly backwards. (3) A north pole withdrawn from above the loop: downward flux is falling, so the induced field points downward, the upper face is a SOUTH pole, and it attracts the receding magnet - the loop repels an approaching pole and attracts a receding one, both from the same rule. Energy check: the force always resists what you are doing, so your hand's work is what appears as I^2*R; if it attracted an approaching magnet the magnet would accelerate in, drive more current, and be attracted harder - unlimited energy from one push, which is the impossibility the minus sign records. (4) Rod L = 0.25 m at v = 3.0 m/s, B = 0.40 T into the page, R = 1.5 ohm: emf = BLv = 0.30 V, I = 0.20 A, area growing so induced field out of the page and current COUNTERCLOCKWISE, F = BIL = 0.020 N against v. Reverse the motion and the current reverses, so F is again against v; P_mech = Fv = 0.060 W = I^2*R = 0.060 W either way. The wrong approach fixes the current from the picture once and keeps it when the motion reverses, manufacturing power. In all four cases the field's direction alone predicted nothing - only whether the flux was rising or falling did.

recapCandidates.topic: Every radius in a solid of revolution is a DISTANCE FROM THE AXIS, not a value of the function, and the integrand is a cross-sectional AREA - so a washer subtracts squared radii, pi*(R^2 - r^2), never pi*(R - r)^2; moving the axis to y = k makes every radius |f(x) - k| without changing the formula; and a shell carries ONE power of its radius with a 2*pi in front, because it is a rolled-up rectangle, not a disc.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: Last week's area-between-curves habit - subtract first, integrate second - carries straight over and produces pi*(R - r)^2, which is algebraically clean and geometrically meaningless, while R and r get read off the functions instead of measured from the axis.
whyQuestions: Why is the thing inside the integral pi*[f(x)]^2 rather than f(x) - what does that expression measure, and what are its units before dx is attached?
Why is the washer pi*integral(R^2 - r^2)dx and not pi*integral(R - r)^2 dx, when for AREAS between curves last week you did subtract before integrating?
Why is R the distance from the axis to the far boundary rather than simply the value of the function - and what does R become when the axis is the line y = k instead of y = 0?
Why does the shell formula carry 2*pi and only one power of the radius, when the disc formula carries pi and two - and where does each factor come from geometrically?
Why can the same solid be computed by washers in y and by shells in x and give the same number, and what feature of a region decides which of the two is actually workable?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
Identifies the integrand as a CROSS-SECTIONAL AREA and the integral as V = integral A(s) ds: slicing perpendicular to the axis gives a full circle (disc, A = pi*R^2) when the region touches the axis and an annulus (washer, A = pi*R^2 - pi*r^2) when it does not - a difference of two circle areas, which is why the radii are squared before subtracting.
Defines R and r as distances measured FROM THE AXIS to the far and near boundaries, and shows that this one definition already handles a shifted axis, R = |f(x) - k| for the axis y = k, so no new formula is needed when the axis moves.
Derives the shell rather than reciting it: a strip PARALLEL to the axis at distance rho, height h, thickness dx sweeps a cylinder that unrolls into a rectangle 2*pi*rho long, so dV = 2*pi*rho*h*dx - one power of rho, and the 2*pi is a circumference; and states that disc/washer needs the axis outside the region's interior or the slices overlap and the region must be split.
recapCandidates.workedExample: One region - between y = x and y = x^2 on [0, 1] - rotated about four axes; only the axis moves. (1) About the x-axis, washers: R = x, r = x^2, V = pi*integral_0^1 (x^2 - x^4)dx = 2*pi/15. The wrong approach, pi*integral_0^1 (x - x^2)^2 dx = pi/30, is four times too small and looks perfectly reasonable - positive, has a pi, integrates cleanly; nothing but understanding catches it. (2) About the y-axis, shells: radius x, height x - x^2, V = 2*pi*integral_0^1 x(x - x^2)dx = pi/6. The wrong approach squares the shell radius by analogy with the disc; check the structure instead - length 2*pi*x times height (x - x^2) times thickness dx, one power of x from the circumference. (3) About y = -1, washers with a shifted axis: R = x + 1 and r = x^2 + 1, V = pi*integral_0^1 [(x + 1)^2 - (x^2 + 1)^2]dx = pi*integral_0^1 (2x - x^2 - x^4)dx = 7*pi/15. The wrong approach keeps R = x, r = x^2 and "adds the shift at the end", or notices that R - r = x - x^2 and concludes the shift cancels; it does not, because squaring first and subtracting second is not subtracting first - the same error as (1) in a new hat. The volume grew from 2*pi/15 to 7*pi/15, and moving the axis away from the region must increase it: that is the cheap check. (4) About x = 2, shells with a shifted axis: the region lies to the LEFT of the axis so radius = 2 - x, positive throughout, height x - x^2, V = 2*pi*integral_0^1 (2 - x)(x - x^2)dx = pi/2. The wrong approach, radius = x - 2, is negative across the region and returns -pi/2 - the one error in this topic the arithmetic does announce, so re-read the geometry instead of taking a modulus at the end. Four axes, four answers: 2*pi/15, pi/6, 7*pi/15, pi/2. Nothing changed but the distance from each boundary to the axis, which is all R, r and the shell radius have ever meant.
